headline_marked: [[Brain-to-text decoder rebuilt]] reducing word errors from 50% to 23.5%
headline: Brain-to-text decoder rebuilt reducing word errors from 50% to 23.5%
summary: A reanalysis of neural data from a speech BCI significantly cut word error rates, improving accuracy for those unable to speak. The model trained in five hours on CPUs, showing substantial gains.
details: Researchers rebuilt a brain-to-text decoder, dramatically reducing its word error rate from 50.0% to 23.5% on 880 test sentences. This reanalysis of neural data from a speech BCI for people who can no longer speak was trained on CPUs in about five hours.

The decoder was built using neural data from a participant with ALS, recorded over 24 days, available through a Dryad release. It utilized activity from 128 electrodes in the motor cortex, processing 256 features per 20 ms bin.

Key improvements involved shrinking the GRU from 5 layers/1,024 units to 3 layers/512 units, reducing parameters to 37.8 million. Grouping sentences by length also cut padding, speeding up batch processing from 11.7s to 1.5s.

Initially, greedy phoneme decoding with silence splitting resulted in 50.0% word errors. Integrating Claude Sonnet 4.6 to select sentences from top five phoneme strings reduced errors to 39.2%, though results were uneven.

A 'guard' mechanism was introduced to prevent the LLM from generating plausible but incorrect sentences when its word count differed significantly. The most effective fix involved direct word decoding with a lexicon and 3-gram language model, providing 10 best sequences to the LLM.

The 3-gram language model, built from training sentences, significantly improved accuracy, with 297 of 880 sentences decoded exactly right. A Tatoeba-based LM, matching conversational style, proved more effective than LibriSpeech's.

The final reported held-out word error rate is 23.0% after splitting the test set for development and evaluation. Future improvements are expected to come from better acoustic and language models, rather than just smarter candidate selection.
